newsitem.title: SLOVAKIA: Slovak prospects bleak after poll chaos - diplomats.
newsitem.headline: Slovak prospects bleak after poll chaos - diplomats.

text.p: The failure of a referendum seen as a test of democracy appears to have buried hopes of Slovakia's joining Western structures in the foreseeable future, diplomats said on Tuesday.
The plebescites were billed as a last chance for Slovakia, which has come under fire from the West for its lack of democratic reforms, for an invitation to join NATO.

Instead, the vote was turned into chaos by Prime Minister Meciar's long-running feud with President Michal Kovac who wanted a question about presidential elections on the ballot and prompted a boycott when it was struck off at the last moment.
"It is all so very sad because it will also take years for any other government to clear the damage," one diplomat from a EU state said. "Poisoned wells take years to clean."

Slovakia's widely boycotted weekend referendum was declared officially void on Monday by the Central Referendum Committee which denounced ballot papers distributed by the Interior Ministry as a "massive swindle".
Within hours, Foreign Minister Pavol Hamzik, charged with persuading Western capitals that Slovakia was progressing towards EU and NATO integration tendered his resignation.
Hamzik cited domestic political events "especially circumstances surrounding the referendum" as making it difficult for him "to pursue the foreign policy priorities of our nation".
"I think this just showed that a professional diplomat such as Hamzik just came to the conclusion that there was no more he could do, and he threw in the towel," another diplomat said.
Meciar on Sunday blamed the referendum's failure on Kovac and the opposition.
"Regardless of whose fault, this was an absolutely negative signal," the diplomat said.

"The fact that a big majority of the 10 percent of the population who turned out for the referendum voted against NATO membership, regardless of whether the vote was valid or not, is a bad signal for NATO... Those further away are not interested in the details, they just see the result."
The central referendum committee refused even to count the result, saying the small number of voters who went to the polls on Friday and Saturday wasted their time because the ballots were illegal.
Kovac and his supporters want future presidents elected directly, a change that might head off the ambitions of Meciar, who could inherit presidential powers if the choice remains with parliament.
Interior Minister Gustav Krajci removed the election question from the ballots at the last minute, claiming the Constitutional Court had declared it illegal.
The government tried to go ahead with the remaining ballot asking whether Slovaks want to join NATO. But many thousands of electors followed the president in refusing to take part.
"These were police state methods," one of the diplomats said. "But it showed that the people have finally had enough of the whole circus."
EU Foreign and Security Policy Commissioner Hans Van Den Broek is due in Bratislava later this week ahead of a final assessment of Slovakia's eligibility to join the EU to be carried out next month.
Diplomats agreed that Van Den Broek was unlikely to bring any message from the EU but noted he was coming at the worst possible time for Slovakia.
"I cannot see him going home with any positive impressions," one of the diplomats said.
